newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus leader takes domestic battle to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader takes domestic battle to Russia.

text.p: Embattled Belarussian president Alexander Lukashenko took his fight against his political foes to the Russian parliament on Wednesday, provoking a walkout by liberal deputies.

Lukashenko, locked in a struggle with his own parliament at home, got a warm welcome from most Russian deputies who share his nostalgia for the Soviet Union and desire for closer integration between the two neighbouring states.

He proposed a joint session of the Russian and Belarussian parliaments in January to consider further moves towards union but did not fulfil predictions in the Moscow press that he would urge a confederation of the two countries.
Last April Lukashenko and President Boris Yeltsin agreed to link Belarus and Russia in a "community" but Lukashenko said that since then the project had failed to make progress.
He told his audience it was "now or never" for the seven-month-old partnership. "Either we get our community on its feet or we discredit the very idea of integration," he said.
As he began his speech to the Duma, Russia's lower house, liberal deputies from the Yabloko party walked out.

Yabloko leader Grigory Yavlinsky warned that there was a danger of a repetition in Belarus of the violent clashes between Russia's president and parliament in Moscow in October 1993. But his proposal to postpone the invitation to Lukashenko to speak was voted down by a large majority.

Belarussians will vote on November 24 in a referendum in which Lukashenko is seeking to broaden his powers while parliament wants to restrict them. "It is in fact a vote of confidence in Lukashenko," he said.
The country's top electoral officer described Lukashenko's referendum on Monday as a "national disgrace" and accused the president of violating the law.
Lukashenko said an alliance of his opponents, Western countries and some influential individuals in Russia were trying to use pressure against him, but did not name any names.
He coupled his attacks on the West and NATO with complaints about Russian newspapers and TV, which he said were spreading slander and disinformation about him.
Economic reformers in Russia believe full union with Belarus would be against Moscow's interests because of the weak state of its economy and the lack of progress towards a free market there.

But Lukashenko indignantly denied this, saying lack of privatisation in Belarus did not mean the economy was in poor shape. " You go into any of our food shops and you will see quality home produce on sale, not "bush legs'," he said,
"Bush legs" is Russian slang for imported chicken legs from the United States which appeared in the shops in large quantities in the early 1990s when George Bush was the U.S. president.

Lukashenko denied that Belarus was a liability to Russia because of its debts for oil and gas, arguing that Moscow was saving money in other areas paid for by his government, such as border and customs patrols.

He also angrily rejected charges by his foes that he was trying to turn his country into a dictatorship. "Among the allies of Russia Belarus is the country with the most stable internal political situation," he said, arguing that he had tried to compromise with his opponents.
"I will have no more powers than the president of Russia or of the United States or other countries," he said.
